pages.x: In Europe, books were copied by hand, and a Bible could take a scribe more than a year. Only churches, universities and the rich owned books. In China, printing from carved wooden blocks was centuries old: the oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, was made in 868.
Around 1040 a Chinese craftsman, Bi Sheng, made movable type from baked clay. Korean printers cast type in metal and in 1377 printed the Jikji, the oldest book made with metal type that survives.
pages.fx: But Chinese writing has thousands of characters, and the idea spread slowly. Europe, with an alphabet of a few dozen letters, was different.

pages.x: Around 1440 Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith, began working on printing, first in Strasbourg, then in his home town of Mainz. He cast letters in a metal mix that melted easily, made an oily ink that clung to metal, and adapted a wine press to print a whole page at once.

His great work, finished around 1455, was a Latin Bible of 1,282 pages in two columns, as handsome as any written by hand. About 180 copies were printed, and 49 survive. A future pope who saw pages wrote that they could be read without glasses.

Gutenberg had borrowed heavily from a merchant, Johann Fust, who sued him in 1455 and took over the workshop. Fust and Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schöffer became successful printers. Gutenberg died in 1468, not rich.
Printing spread like fire. By 1500 there were presses in some 250 towns across Europe, and they had printed perhaps 20 million books. A book was now far cheaper, and every copy was the same.

In 1517 Martin Luther's attacks on the Church were printed and spread across Germany in weeks. He called printing God's highest gift. Without the press, the Reformation might have been crushed like earlier protests.

Printing made knowledge cheap, lasting and the same in every copy. It spread the Renaissance, the Reformation and the new science, fixed the spelling of languages and helped millions learn to read. Many call it the most important invention of the last thousand years.
